docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Tests come in three sizes, set by what a test uses rather than by how long it happens to take. The size decides where it runs.

size marker what a test may use where it runs budget small none one process, memory, tmp_path a plain pytest; CI on every push, Python 3.11 to 3.14 the whole tier within 60 s on a laptop medium medium another process, video files, a compile that needs gigabytes CI on every push, Python 3.11 and 3.14, after the small tier small and medium within 10 min on CI large large closed-loop rollouts at the scored length, many seeds CI on merges to main, one interpreter each test within 15 min

records is not a size. Those tests check that the recorded baselines still describe this tree, and they run in a job of their own, so a stale record fails that job alone and a failing test job always means a real bug.

agent is not a size either. Those tests need stable-baselines3 and torch, the opt-in agent group, and skip without it. The README's SAC example is one. CI's agent job installs the group and runs them, and fails if any of them skips:

uv sync --group dev --group agent
pytest -m agent

learning is not a size either. Those tests train a short PPO on one task per group and check that it ends up better than the best constant action on seeds it never saw, which is the bar the PID meets. PPO comes from Ajax, the opt-in learning group. Ajax needs JAX 0.10 or later, so the tests run on Python 3.14 and skip elsewhere. CI's learning job fails if any of them skips:

uv sync --python 3.14 --group dev --group learning
pytest -m learning

pytest                   # small, on every core
pytest -m medium -n 2    # medium; two workers keep two big compiles in memory
pytest -m large          # large
pytest -m records        # records
pytest -m ""             # everything

A later -m replaces the default one, and -n0 runs serially, which --pdb needs.

Every run ends with its 15 slowest tests, so a test that outgrows its size shows up there before it shows up in the budget.

docs.title: Which size a new test is
docs.text:
Start small. A small test that is slow is a design problem first, and the usual cause is stepping a plant from Python: run it inside jax.lax.scan or jax.lax.while_loop, jit the step, and shorten episodes and shapes to what the property needs. That is how the glass furnace and boiler drum tests went from 125 s and 44 s to a few seconds without changing an assertion.

Mark it medium when it starts another process (subprocess, or moviepy running ffmpeg to write a video), or when it compiles an aircraft planner or gradient tuner. Those compiles peak at 2.5 to 5 GB and take up to three minutes on a cold cache; four at once shut CI runners down on 2026-10-27.

Mark it large when the property only shows at the scored length: a closed loop that holds its target, a PID that beats the best constant action, a check over many seeds.

docs.title: Where a test goes
docs.text:
Each test should be able to fail because of a real bug, and anything true of all environments is checked in one place.

  • tests/test_env_conformance.py owns every contract that applies to all environments: shapes, spaces, the clock, keys, finiteness, jit and vmap. A new environment inherits it by registering. A task that does not meet a contract yet goes in a KNOWN_* table with its reason, which makes the check a strict xfail for that task, so fixing the gap fails until its entry goes.
  • An environment's own folder holds its physics and its bounds: published values, emergent behaviour, its limits and how its actions map onto them.
  • Tests that restate configuration go. A test that compares a setting with the same number typed again fails only when someone edits it on purpose.
  • Guards against mistakes that cannot be undone stay, even though they only fail on an edit, as in tests/test_release_workflow.py. A published version or a leaked token cannot be taken back.

docs.title: The expensive measurement is recorded, not reproduced
docs.text:
Checking that each shipped MPC really is an upper bound on its PID meant rolling sixteen controllers out on five seeds: about forty minutes of CPU, and [plane] alone was 836 s. Because pytest-xdist distributes across tests and not within one, that single test set roughly 70% of the large job's wall-clock floor and came close to its 30-minute timeout on CI's slower cores.

It is now recorded by hand into src/target_gym/data/baseline_returns/ and asserted from there, guarded by a fingerprint that refuses a record whose code has moved. See Baselines for the design and the reasoning behind fingerprinting source rather than behaviour.

make baselines           # re-measure everything, ~40 min
make baselines-plane     # or just one environment

Run it when a test tells you a record is stale, and commit the result with the change that invalidated it.

docs.title: XLA compilations are cached, in the process and between runs
docs.text:
What remained was not stepping the plants but compiling them. Reverse-mode through an RK4 aircraft builds a large graph, and it showed: a tuner smoke test that takes two gradient steps still cost 45 s, and shrinking its problem from 36 target pairs and 2000 steps to 2 and 100 barely moved it. The graph was the cost, not the rollout.

JAX can persist compiled executables to disk, keyed on the computation itself. tests/conftest.py points it at .jax_cache, which does two things at once: under xdist it stops every worker compiling the same graph, and in CI actions/cache restores it between runs, so compilation becomes a once-per-code-change cost rather than once-per-push.

Measured on the whole fast suite: 217 s cold, 34.5 s warm. On one tuner test alone, 44.9 s against 3.4 s. The cache is about 51 MB.

A stale entry is never wrongly reused -- entries are keyed by the jaxpr, the backend and the JAX version, so a changed computation simply misses. The CI key includes a hash of src/, with a looser restore-keys prefix so a code change still seeds from the previous cache instead of starting empty.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Coverage is gated at 89% over the small tier alone, so moving a test to medium or large removes it from the gate. Check the number before doing it.
  • strict=True on every xfail. A known defect that gets fixed must fail the suite until its annotation is updated, so the record cannot quietly rot.

docs.title: Using the tuned PIDs
docs.text: Every environment ships a tuned PID controller. It is the baseline every published number is measured against, so it is useful in three ways: as a working controller to run, as the reference your agent's score is paired against, and as a prior to build learning on. This page shows where to get it, how to run it, how to evaluate against it, and how to plug it into training.

docs.title: Where to get one
docs.text:
target_gym.make_expert builds it by registry name:

import target_gym as tg
from target_gym.registry import REGISTRY

expert = tg.make_expert("cstr")

spec = REGISTRY["cstr"]
print(spec.has_pid, spec.baselines_note or "no caveat")

All 24 environments ship one (spec.has_pid is true everywhere). Where a baseline comes with a caveat, spec.baselines_note states it. The gains were tuned by scripts/tune_pid.py and live in src/target_gym/data/pid_gains.json; you do not need to read that file to use them. Baselines describes how each one is structured and tuned.

docs.title: The interface
docs.text:
A PID remembers its integral and its last error. You carry that memory from one step to the next, as you carry the environment's state:

When Call At each episode start memory = expert.reset() Each step action, memory = expert.step(memory, obs) For n environments at once memory = expert.reset(n), then actions, memory = jax.vmap(expert.step)(memory, obs)

The same step runs in a Python loop, under jit and inside lax.scan, on CPU or GPU. It returns the action in the environment's own units, already clipped to its bounds. It reads the observation only, never the hidden state, which is what makes the PID a fair peer for a learned policy. (The MPC reads the true state, so it is an upper bound, not a peer.)

Two rules keep the memory right:

  • Reset it at the start of every episode, or the previous episode's integral leaks in. Under an auto-resetting env.step inside a scan, see Episode boundaries.
  • Keep the memory step returns, once per environment step. Stepping on a replayed or logged observation is harmless as long as you discard the memory it returns.

score_policy, run_suite and env.save_video run a policy in their own loop and take the expert as it is.

docs.title: Running it in a loop
docs.text:
With the keys the scored episodes use:

import jax
import numpy as np
import target_gym as tg
from target_gym.benchmark import episode_keys
from target_gym.registry import REGISTRY

spec = REGISTRY["cstr"]
env = spec.make_env()
params = spec.make_test_params()   # the configuration the baselines are scored on
expert = tg.make_expert("cstr")

# Seed 0's keys as the scored episodes take them: one to reset, a fresh one
# every step.
T = int(params.max_steps_in_episode)
reset_keys, step_keys = episode_keys(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), 1, T)
obs, state = env.reset_env(reset_keys[0], params)
memory = expert.reset()

total = 0.0
for t in range(T):
    action, memory = expert.step(memory, obs)
    obs, state, reward, terminated, _ = env.step_env(step_keys[t, 0], state, action, params)
    total += float(reward)
    if terminated:
        break

print("PID return:", total)

Use spec.make_test_params() rather than the default params. On every aircraft task and the reactor the defaults run a longer episode, and some aircraft tasks also set a different reference, so only the test params reproduce the scored numbers.

docs.title: Episode returns, paired on seeds
docs.text:
The recorded PID returns are in src/target_gym/data/baseline_returns/, one per seed. runners.rollout is the loop they were recorded with, so running your policy through it on the same seeds gives a paired comparison without re-running the PID:

import numpy as np
from target_gym.provenance import load_recorded_baselines
from target_gym.registry import REGISTRY
from target_gym.runners.runners import baseline_policy, rollout

spec = REGISTRY["cstr"]
params = spec.make_test_params()
recorded = load_recorded_baselines()["cstr"]
seeds = range(recorded["seeds"])


def episode_return(make_policy, seed):
    return float(np.sum(rollout(spec, params, make_policy(), seed=seed)[2]))


# A fresh, reset PID per episode reproduces the recorded returns exactly.
pid_returns = [episode_return(lambda: baseline_policy(spec, "pid", params), s) for s in seeds]
assert np.allclose(pid_returns, recorded["pid_returns"])

# Your policy goes in the same slot: any callable obs -> action
# (or (obs, state) -> action) built fresh for each episode.
mine = [episode_return(lambda: baseline_policy(spec, "pid", params), s) for s in seeds]
wins = sum(m > p for m, p in zip(mine, recorded["pid_returns"]))
print(f"beats the PID on {wins} of {len(mine)} seeds")

docs.title: The protocol score
docs.text:
Returns mix the cost of reaching a target with the cost of holding it, in a proportion set by the episode length. The RL protocol scores a policy against the expert on three numbers: how many times cheaper it is over the episode (ratio, with the share of seeds it wins), where it sits between the expert (0) and the ceiling (1) while holding (score), and how much room the task leaves (headroom, in decades). One call runs your policy and the expert on the same seeds:

import target_gym as tg

policy = tg.make_expert("cstr")      # swap in your own: policy(obs) -> action
m = tg.score_policy("cstr", policy, seeds=3)   # 10 for a result
print(f"{m['ratio']:.3g}x cheaper than the expert on {m['win_rate']:.0%} of seeds")
print(f"score {m['score']:.2f}, room {m['headroom']:.2f} decades")

With the expert itself in the slot, the ratio comes out at 1 and the score at 0. A score of nan means the expert already tracks within the instrument's resolution, so the task has no room to score.

docs.title: As a residual base
docs.text:
The structure the RL protocol treats as primary: the agent learns a bounded correction on top of the PID, so a zero correction recovers the PID exactly.

import numpy as np
import target_gym as tg
from target_gym.registry import REGISTRY

spec = REGISTRY["cstr"]
env, params = spec.make_env(), spec.make_test_params()
space = env.action_space(params)
low, high = np.asarray(space.low), np.asarray(space.high)
alpha = 0.25 * (high - low) / 2      # the correction spans a quarter of the range


def residual_step(expert, correction):
    """``correction(obs)`` is your network's output, in [-1, 1]."""

    def step(memory, obs):
        action, memory = expert.step(memory, obs)
        return np.clip(action + alpha * correction(obs), low, high), memory

    return step


expert = tg.make_expert("cstr")
step = residual_step(expert, lambda obs: np.zeros_like(low))   # untrained: the PID
memory = expert.reset()

The protocol sweeps the scale over 0.1, 0.25 and 1.0 and reports all three, so a reader can tell "learning improved the PID" from "learning ignored it".

Because the PID has memory, three things matter for a residual agent:

  • Store the PID's action with each transition. It depends on the PID's memory, not only on obs, so recomputing it from a replayed observation gives a different action.
  • Feed the PID's action to the network. The integral is not in obs, so without it the agent cannot see what the base is about to do.
  • Watch for windup at large scales. The PID cannot see the correction. When the correction pushes the sum past a bound, the PID's integral keeps growing. At zero correction it is exactly the PID.

docs.title: As demonstrations
docs.text:
To pre-fill a replay buffer or pretrain by behavioural cloning, record the PID's own transitions:

import jax
import numpy as np
import target_gym as tg
from target_gym.registry import REGISTRY

spec = REGISTRY["cstr"]
env, params = spec.make_env(), spec.make_test_params()
expert = tg.make_expert("cstr")

transitions = []
for seed in range(3):
    key, reset_key = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(seed))
    obs, state = env.reset(reset_key, params)
    memory = expert.reset()
    for _ in range(params.max_steps_in_episode):
        key, step_key = jax.random.split(key)   # a fresh key every step
        action, memory = expert.step(memory, obs)
        next_obs, state, reward, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(step_key, state, action, params)
        transitions.append((np.asarray(obs), np.asarray(action), float(reward), np.asarray(next_obs)))
        obs = next_obs
        if terminated or truncated:
            break

print(len(transitions), "transitions")

docs.title: Inside a jitted loop, on GPU
docs.text:
A fully jitted learner (a jax.lax.scan over environment steps, as in PureJaxRL-style agents) keeps the expert's memory in the scan's carry, which is where the integral lives. It matches the scored host PID up to float32 rounding, close enough to reproduce the recorded returns, as the example checks.

import jax
import numpy as np
import target_gym as tg
from target_gym.benchmark import episode_keys
from target_gym.provenance import load_recorded_baselines
from target_gym.registry import REGISTRY

spec = REGISTRY["cstr"]
env, params = spec.make_env(), spec.make_test_params()
expert = tg.make_expert("cstr")


def episode_return(key):
    # The scored episodes' keys: one to reset, a fresh one every step.
    reset_keys, step_keys = episode_keys(key, 1, int(params.max_steps_in_episode))
    obs, env_state = env.reset_env(reset_keys[0], params)

    def step(carry, step_key):
        obs, env_state, memory = carry
        action, memory = expert.step(memory, obs)
        obs, env_state, reward, _, _ = env.step_env(step_key, env_state, action, params)
        return (obs, env_state, memory), reward

    carry = (obs, env_state, expert.reset())
    _, rewards = jax.lax.scan(step, carry, step_keys[:, 0])
    return rewards.sum()


keys = jax.numpy.stack([jax.random.PRNGKey(s) for s in range(10)])
returns = jax.jit(jax.vmap(episode_return))(keys)   # ten episodes at once

recorded = load_recorded_baselines()["cstr"]["pid_returns"]
assert np.allclose(returns, recorded, rtol=1e-3)     # the host-scored numbers

For a batch of environments, expert.reset(n) and jax.vmap(expert.step) do the same with one memory per environment, as in the next example.

docs.title: Episode boundaries
docs.text:
Nothing resets the memory inside a scan for you. env.step restarts an environment when its episode ends, but the memory you carry keeps the old integral unless you reset it too. reset_where_done does that, for one environment or a batch:

import jax
import target_gym as tg
from target_gym.experts import reset_where_done
from target_gym.registry import REGISTRY

spec = REGISTRY["cstr"]
env, params = spec.make_env(), spec.make_test_params()
expert, num_envs = tg.make_expert("cstr"), 4
key, reset_key = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(0))
obs, env_state = jax.vmap(env.reset, in_axes=(0, None))(
    jax.random.split(reset_key, num_envs), params
)
step_all = jax.vmap(env.step, in_axes=(0, 0, 0, None))
expert_all = jax.vmap(expert.step)


def step(carry, step_key):
    obs, env_state, memory = carry
    actions, memory = expert_all(memory, obs)
    keys = jax.random.split(step_key, num_envs)   # a fresh key every step
    obs, env_state, reward, terminated, truncated, _ = step_all(keys, env_state, actions, params)
    # env.step has already restarted the environments that finished; restart their PIDs too.
    memory = reset_where_done(terminated | truncated, memory, expert.reset())
    return (obs, env_state, memory), reward


carry = (obs, env_state, expert.reset(num_envs))
n_steps = 2 * int(params.max_steps_in_episode)   # two episodes per environment
run = jax.jit(lambda c, k: jax.lax.scan(step, c, jax.random.split(k, n_steps)))
_, rewards = run(carry, key)

For a single environment, pass a scalar done. Reset on terminated | truncated only: in a continuing environment a trip restarts the plant without raising either flag, and the PID keeps its memory through it, as the scored baselines do.

docs.title: Formation
docs.text:
Fly a lead and two wingmen in a V, every aircraft controlled by the policy. The lead holds an altitude and a heading that follows a patrol route, and each wingman holds a slot fixed in the lead's frame. Because the lead is learned too, each wingman's reference is a co-player rather than a script; the team shares one cost, and a collision between any two aircraft trips all three. The action is the three aircraft's controls, the lead's first.

docs.title: Four-tank
docs.text:
Hold the levels of the two lower tanks of Johansson's quadruple-tank process with two pumps. Each pump sends most of its flow to the upper tank on the other side, which drains into the opposite lower tank, so pairing each pump with the tank below it is the wrong move and the response is non-minimum phase. All four levels are measured: the difficulty is the coupling, not what is seen.

docs.title: Patrol - wingman, bearing-only
docs.text:
The patrol task flown from a passive sensor: the wingman sees range, azimuth and elevation to the lead instead of the lead's relative state. docs.title: Baselines
docs.text:
Recorded over 10 seeds of the 200-step episode (see Baseline results). The reward is a cost, so a return closer to zero is better.

controller mean return cost per step PID -3.644e+04 182.2 MPC -3907 19.54

The MPC beats the PID on 10 of 10 seeds and does not trip the plant on any of them.

The PID is a lead-state estimator feeding the same formation hold the full-observation variant uses. Range with azimuth and elevation is a complete relative-position measurement, so the only unobservable quantity is the lead's heading, which the slot needs because it is expressed in the lead's frame; the estimator takes the lead's velocity from the follower's own and the change in the relative position, and its heading from that track less the crab the follower flies in the same air. The MPC slot holds patrol's oracle reading the true state, so it is a full-state bound, not a bearing-only controller. On a task defined by what the observation withholds, its score measures information and control together: what the hidden lead state is worth plus what a policy leaves on the table. It never reads the observation, so its per-step costs equal patrol's seed for seed.

docs.title: pH neutralisation
docs.text:
Hold the pH of a stirred tank, where strong acid meets strong base in a carbonate buffer, at a target by setting the base flow. docs.title: Baseline results
docs.text:
Every environment ships two reference controllers, scored on its test configuration (spec.make_test_params()):

  • The expert (the "pid" slot): reads the observation only, as your agent does. It is the score to beat.
  • The oracle (the "mpc" slot): reads the true state, including what the observation hides. It shows what information and planning are worth.

Costs on this page are per step, lower is better, in each environment's own units. To score your own policy, see Evaluating against it. How the controllers are built and measured is in How the baselines work.

docs.text: How many times cheaper the oracle holds each target than the expert, and where the ceiling sits: tracking every quantity within its instrument's resolution. Switch the anchor to the ceiling to see how far each controller is from as good as a real plant can verify. Hover a row for the numbers, including the whole episode.

docs.title: Room to grow
docs.text:
Hold is the tracking cost per step once a controller has settled on each target, after a settle fixed per environment. The ceiling is tracking every quantity within its instrument's resolution: as good as a real plant can verify. Room is the number of decades from the expert's hold down to the ceiling; 0 means the expert is already there. The oracle score places the oracle between the expert (0) and the ceiling (1). Score a policy the same way with target_gym.scoring.score_policy. 3 seeds each.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• patrol_bearing_only: The PID is a lead-state estimator feeding the same formation hold the full-observation variant uses. Range with azimuth and elevation is a complete relative-position measurement, so the only unobservable quantity is the lead's heading, which the slot needs because it is expressed in the lead's frame; the estimator takes the lead's velocity from the follower's own and the change in the relative position, and its heading from that track less the crab the follower flies in the same air. The MPC slot holds patrol's oracle reading the true state, so it is a full-state bound, not a bearing-only controller. On a task defined by what the observation withholds, its score measures information and control together: what the hidden lead state is worth plus what a policy leaves on the table. It never reads the observation, so its per-step costs equal patrol's seed for seed.
  • formation: The PID flies the lead seat as a formation lead: the 3D heading task's course hold and pitch on height, aimed at the heading the route commands, at a set power, so its wingmen have a steady reference. Each wingman seat flies the patrol's formation hold. The MPC slot is the patrol oracle's design applied to the whole formation: the patrol's lead autopilot in the lead seat and its twin-autopilot law in each wingman seat, with one residual planner over every seat on the team cost.
